Field surveys of Barrens topminnow populations in the Caney Fork system reveal that individuals attain a maximum standard length of 5.5 cm [Li = 5.5 cm], a modest size typical of fundulid species adapted to spring-fed headwater habitats. This ultimate length is achieved through a growth trajectory that slows markedly after the onset of reproductive maturity. At puberty, which is characterized by the first appearance of differentiated gonadal tissue, males and females measure approximately 3.9 cm [Lp = approximately 3.9 cm] in standard length, a threshold that corresponds roughly to 70 percent of the species' asymptotic body size. The transition from juvenile to reproductively competent adult is tightly linked to thermal regime, as individuals developing in cooler spring runs exhibit delayed maturation compared to those in warmer peripheral pools. Growth increments derived from otolith microstructural analysis indicate that the first year of life is the period of most rapid somatic expansion, with daily length increases averaging 0.2 to 0.3 mm during the initial summer growing season.

Embryonic development in Fundulus julisia proceeds rapidly under controlled laboratory conditions. When eggs are maintained at a constant temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C], hatching occurs after approximately 8.3 days [ab = approximately 8.3 days], a relatively short incubation period that reflects the small egg size and reduced yolk volume characteristic of this species. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva, still largely transparent and only a few millimeters in total length, carries an endogenous nutritional reserve that sustains it through the first days of exogenous feeding transition. The duration from fertilization to eclosion is markedly temperature-dependent: at 23 °C [T = 23 °C], chorionase secretion and subsequent chorion rupture are completed within the same 8- to 9-day window observed consistently across multiple experimental trials. Post-hatching, the prolarva remains largely sedentary, adhering to submerged vegetation via cement glands until the yolk sac is nearly resorbed, at which point mouth opening and active prey capture commence. The abbreviated embryonic phase is ecologically significant, as it allows multiple spawning events within a single breeding season and reduces the vulnerability window of demersal eggs to predation by aquatic invertebrates.

The wet weight at birth for a newly hatched Barrens topminnow larva is approximately 0.0064 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0064 grams], derived from the volume of the fertilized egg which measures 2.3 mm in diameter. This minimal body mass places the species at the lower end of the size spectrum among North American fundulids and imposes constraints on early larval feeding ecology, as the small gape limits initial prey items to rotifers and early-stage copepod nauplii. In contrast, the ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult reaches 2.04 grams [Wwi = 2.04 grams], representing a more than three-hundredfold increase in somatic mass from the neonatal stage. This substantial growth trajectory is supported by a diet composed primarily of aquatic insect larvae, microcrustaceans, and occasional terrestrial fallout, with the underlying length-weight relationship conforming to a power function typical of fusiform teleosts. The conversion from total length to body mass follows an allometric exponent that reflects the relatively deep-bodied morphology of mature individuals compared to the slender, elongate profile of juveniles. Field-caught specimens exceeding 2.04 grams are rare and typically represent large, gravid females just prior to spawning.

Reproductive output in Barrens topminnow has been quantified through controlled spawning experiments under simulated spring thermal regimes. At a temperature of 26.5 °C [T = 26.5 °C], approximating peak summer conditions in the species' headwater habitat, gravid females deposit clutches at regular intervals. Each clutch contains approximately 4 to 6 eggs [N_R_i = Each clutch contains approximately 4 to 6 eggs], and females produce approximately 1 clutch every 3 to 5 days [F_R_i = approximately 1 clutch every 3 to 5 days] under optimal conditions, yielding a cumulative seasonal fecundity that can exceed several hundred eggs per female. This iteroparous reproductive strategy, paired with the adhesive demersal eggs that are attached to submerged vegetation, allows for repeated spawning events that buffer against stochastic egg mortality from fluctuating spring flows or sudden temperature drops. The high thermal optimum of 26.5 °C for reproductive activity is consistent with the species' restriction to spring-fed systems that maintain relatively stable water temperatures year-round.

Longitudinal field data from mark-recapture studies indicate that the time since birth at death for Barrens topminnow in natural populations is approximately 3 years [am = approximately 3 years], representing the maximum documented lifespan for the species in its native spring habitats at a temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C]. This longevity was recorded at a water temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C], reflecting the stable thermal conditions characteristic of the primary spring pool where the oldest individuals were collected. The age structure of wild populations reveals that most mortality occurs during the first year, with annual survival rates increasing substantially after individuals surpass the 3.9 cm standard length at puberty threshold. Senescence in this species is marked by a gradual decline in body condition, fin ray deterioration, and reduced gonadal investment in older age classes. The three-year lifespan is relatively short compared to some congeners from more stable lentic environments, but is consistent with the high metabolic demands imposed by the species' active foraging lifestyle in cool, well-oxygenated spring runs. No individuals older than 3 years have been documented across more than a decade of systematic sampling throughout the species' restricted geographic range.
